title: hyperPad vs Buildbox: Best No-Code Game Engine for iPad Creators
summary: Compare hyperPad and Buildbox for no-code game development: features, pricing, iPad support, classroom use, and publishing, so you can pick the right fit.
body_markdown:
The no-code game engine you pick decides how fast you can prototype, publish, and iterate on your ideas. That choice matters most if you create on a tablet, learn game design as a student, run classroom projects, or want a visual workflow as an indie developer. If that's you, hyperPad and Buildbox are worth comparing closely.


Both tools cut out the complexity of traditional coding. They go about it very differently. hyperPad was designed for game development on iPad, with a touch-first workflow and visual Behaviors. Buildbox focuses on drag-and-drop game creation, mainly on desktop, with export-focused publishing.


This comparison covers strengths, limitations, pricing, publishing, classroom value, and ease of use, so you can decide which one fits your goals.


### Best For


#### hyperPad Best For


- Creators who want to build games entirely on iPad, with no desktop computer
- Students, classrooms, and younger creators learning visual game development
- Quick prototyping with touch controls and visual Behaviors


#### Buildbox Best For


- Desktop-based creators focused on mobile game publishing
- Users building template-driven arcade and hypercasual games
- Developers looking for export options across multiple platforms


## Feature Comparison


## Workflow and Ease of Use


### hyperPad Workflow


hyperPad was built on one idea: you should be able to make a game on the device you have in your hands when an idea hits. It runs natively on iPad with a fully touch-based workflow. You build levels, design interfaces, set up logic, test gameplay, and iterate without switching devices.


The biggest difference is Behaviors. You don't write programming syntax. You connect actions and events to create a flowchart of your game's logic. Beginners can start right away, and there's room to build complex mechanics as you grow.


The workflow feels especially natural for:


- Students
- Teachers
- Younger creators
- Artists moving into game design
- Mobile-first developers


The learning curve is gentle because the interface was designed for touch from the start, instead of adapting a desktop workflow to a tablet.


### Buildbox Workflow


Buildbox uses a drag-and-drop system designed to simplify game creation for non-programmers. It became popular through hypercasual mobile game development and template-based workflows.


You can create mechanics quickly by connecting gameplay systems visually. Buildbox works well for simple arcade games and prototypes, particularly if you already know desktop-based tools.


Buildbox workflows are more desktop-oriented, though. Some companion mobile functionality exists, but the full editor isn't built around creating on iPad.


If you want a fully portable workflow without a laptop or desktop, this distinction matters.


## iPad Experience Comparison


### Why iPad-First Development Matters


Tablets have changed what creators expect from creative tools. More and more, you want to sketch ideas, prototype games, and publish projects from one portable device.


hyperPad was built around that. Every interaction is designed for touch:


- Level editing
- Physics placement
- Behaviors
- UI building
- Asset management
- Testing gameplay


The result feels closer to digital sketching than to traditional software development.


Buildbox is user-friendly, but it still carries many assumptions from desktop software. You'll often rely on a mouse and keyboard and a desktop publishing pipeline.


If portability is your priority, hyperPad gives you a more complete tablet workflow.


### Which Platform Is Better for Mobile Creators?


If your goal is to:


- Build games on the couch
- Prototype while traveling
- Teach in classrooms using iPads
- Create without a desktop setup
- Work directly with touch controls


hyperPad has a clear advantage.


If your workflow already revolves around desktop software and export pipelines, Buildbox may fit your existing habits better.


## Educational and Classroom Use


### hyperPad for Education


hyperPad works well in schools because it lowers the technical barrier while still teaching core game design concepts.


Students can learn:


- Logic systems
- Game mechanics
- Level design
- Problem solving
- Interactive storytelling
- UI and UX basics
- Physics-based gameplay


The touch-first workflow helps younger students stay engaged. They spend their time on creativity and experimentation instead of fighting a complex interface.


Teachers get:


- Faster onboarding
- Visual learning
- Less setup
- Device portability
- Room for collaborative classroom projects


iPads are already common in schools, so hyperPad fits into the devices you likely have. Educational institutions get 50% off through Apple School Manager, with Private Login for student accounts.


### Buildbox for Education


Buildbox can also work in classrooms, particularly in programs focused on entrepreneurship or mobile publishing.


Its desktop-oriented workflow can add setup requirements:


- Computer labs
- Hardware management
- Software installations
- Traditional workstation setups


That adds friction in classrooms where mobility and accessibility are priorities.


## Publishing and Game Creation Capabilities


### hyperPad Publishing Approach


hyperPad focuses on getting you from prototype to published game in one accessible workflow.


You can:


- Build complete 2D games
- Create physics-based mechanics
- Design custom UI
- Import graphics and audio
- Prototype quickly
- Publish your projects to the hyperPad Hub for the community to play


With hyperPad (the paid app), you can also export your game to the App Store. Exporting creates an Xcode project, and you finish the upload on a Mac with Xcode and an Apple Developer account. The app is built for creators who don't come from a traditional programming background.


It works especially well for:


- Platformers
- Puzzle games
- Educational games
- Story-driven games
- Arcade mechanics
- Experimental prototypes


### Buildbox Publishing Approach


Buildbox became well known through the rise of hypercasual mobile games. It supports fast development of arcade-style projects and monetization-focused games.


Creators often use Buildbox for:


- Endless runners
- Simple arcade games
- Casual mobile games
- Prototype-driven publishing


Buildbox's export workflows suit teams already working in desktop development environments.


## Pricing Comparison


### hyperPad Pricing


Pricing is one of the biggest differences between hyperPad and Buildbox.


hyperPad uses a one-time purchase:


- hyperPad Starter is free and includes one project
- hyperPad is a one-time purchase of USD $14.99, which lifts the project limit and adds App Store export
- No monthly subscription
- Schools get 50% off through Apple School Manager
- You keep 100% of the revenue from games you export. hyperPad takes 0%.


This pricing works well for:


- Parents
- Students
- Schools
- Hobbyists
- First-time creators


You pay once instead of committing to an ongoing subscription.


### Buildbox Pricing


Buildbox generally uses subscription-based pricing, which can cost more over time.


Depending on the plan, you may run into:


- Monthly subscriptions
- Feature limitations
- Export restrictions
- Tiered access


For professional studios or monetization-focused developers, a subscription may fit an existing production budget.


For younger creators or school programs, recurring costs are a bigger consideration.

## Performance and Prototyping Speed


### hyperPad Prototyping Speed


hyperPad is built for fast iteration. The whole workflow happens on iPad, so you can:


- Test instantly
- Adjust Behaviors quickly
- Rearrange levels with touch controls
- Prototype interactions fast


That shortens the gap between an idea and a playable game.


For beginners, this matters a lot. Momentum keeps you learning.


### Buildbox Prototyping Speed


Buildbox also supports fast iteration, particularly for arcade mechanics and reusable gameplay templates.


Its workflow can be efficient if you're experienced with desktop pipelines. Switching between desktop editing and testing may feel less immediate than hyperPad's touch-first environment.


## Community and Accessibility


### hyperPad Community


hyperPad supports creators through the hyperPad Hub, where you can publish your projects, play other creators' games, and Branch Open Source projects to see how they work.


It appeals strongly to:


- Young developers
- Student creators
- Teachers
- Mobile-first designers
- Non-programmers


The interface is less intimidating than traditional tools, so you can get from concept to playable prototype faster.


### Buildbox Community


Buildbox has a recognizable presence among indie mobile developers and hypercasual creators.


Its audience often includes:


- Indie studios
- Mobile monetization creators
- Desktop-first developers
- Prototype-focused teams


Both communities offer plenty to learn from. They serve different kinds of creators.


## Which Platform Should You Choose?


### Choose hyperPad If:


- You want to build games entirely on iPad
- You like touch-first workflows
- You are teaching students or kids
- You want a lower upfront cost
- You prefer a one-time purchase
- You are learning game design visually
- You want to create wherever you are


### Choose Buildbox If:


- You already work primarily on desktop
- You focus heavily on mobile publishing pipelines
- You want template-driven arcade workflows
- You are comfortable with subscription pricing
- You prioritize desktop export options


## Final Verdict


hyperPad and Buildbox both reduce the complexity of traditional game development. They target different kinds of creators.


With hyperPad, you make the whole game on iPad with visual Behaviors, and you pay once. It is particularly effective for classrooms, students, beginners, and developers who want a portable no-code workflow.


Buildbox remains a capable option for desktop-oriented mobile game creation, especially if you focus on arcade and hypercasual publishing.


If you want touch-first development, easy classroom setup, and a price you pay once, hyperPad is the approachable choice.


## FAQ


### Is Buildbox available on iPad as a full editor?


Buildbox is primarily designed around desktop workflows. Some mobile functionality may exist, but the complete creation experience is generally desktop-oriented.


### Is hyperPad good for kids learning game design?


Yes. hyperPad suits beginners, students, and younger creators because it uses visual Behaviors and touch-first workflows instead of traditional coding syntax.


### Which platform is faster for prototyping on a tablet?


hyperPad is generally faster for tablet-based prototyping because it was designed for touch on iPad.


### Does hyperPad require a subscription?


No. hyperPad is a one-time purchase of USD $14.99. You can also start with hyperPad Starter, which is free and includes one project.


### Which engine is better for classrooms?


hyperPad is particularly strong for classrooms because it's easy to pick up, fully visual, and runs on the iPads many schools already use. Schools get 50% off through Apple School Manager.


### Can both platforms create mobile games?


Yes. Both hyperPad and Buildbox support mobile game creation, although their workflows and target audiences differ.
